title: Psycho Pete Returns

jokes.text: Wait, so you just painted your butt blue and nobody noticed the hole in your pants? Yeah, it worked, it worked. It's a good trick.
jokes.setup: Cold open mid-conversation implying someone had a wardrobe malfunction they solved by painting their skin
jokes.punchline: The 'trick' of painting your butt blue to hide a hole in your pants is treated as legitimate and clever
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny cold open: dropped into a conversation that reveals absurd logic treated as wisdom. The specificity of 'blue' adds to the absurdity. It's a good scene-setter but not exceptional — it works because of the confidence with which the trick is endorsed.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Wait, so you just painted your butt blue and nobody noticed the hole in your pants?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, it worked, it worked.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's a good trick.

jokes.text: Great song and great news?! Yeah, and it's all tied in with the song, so it makes sense.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have news to announce and they've been playing 'Psycho Killer' by Talking Heads
jokes.punchline: The justification that the news 'ties in' with 'Psycho Killer' is stated with complete earnestness before the reveal
jokes.explanation: The punchline lands retroactively once we know the news. 'It ties in with the song' is a funny bit of narrative self-awareness without being meta. Decent setup for the Psycho Pete reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: The guy you went to high school with, who killed and ate his family?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah... Yeah, yeah, yeah... but don't get all hung up on that, man

jokes.text: We're gonna get our psycho back, bitches.
jokes.setup: Announcement that Psycho Pete, who killed and ate his family, has been released from the mental institution
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis frame reuniting with a cannibal-murderer as a triumphant, exciting event — 'get our psycho back, bitches'
jokes.explanation: The sheer enthusiasm for getting their cannibal friend back is a sharp encapsulation of the gang's moral void. 'Bitches' as the triumphant punctuation is perfectly in character for Mac. Good economy and strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: they unscrambled his brain and he's, like, good now.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, they sorted him out, they sorted him out.

jokes.text: The guy you went to high school with, who killed and ate his family? Yeah... Yeah, yeah... but don't get all hung up on that, man.
jokes.setup: Dee incredulously reminds them what Psycho Pete actually did
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis wave off cannibalism/murder as an irrelevant detail — 'don't get all hung up on that'
jokes.explanation: The dismissal of cannibalism as something not worth 'getting hung up on' is a crisp piece of character comedy. It efficiently reveals everything about how Mac and Dennis prioritize fun over basic human morality. The understatement is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I lived with these maniacs in the loony bin. There is no curing those psycho bastards... but once your brain's a piece of shit, it's always a piece of shit.

jokes.text: It's actually really sad... but once your brain's a piece of shit, it's always a piece of shit.
jokes.setup: Frank claims authority on mental illness from living in the loony bin, then appears to offer compassion ('it's actually really sad')
jokes.punchline: The pivot to 'once your brain's a piece of shit, it's always a piece of shit' — blunt nihilism delivered as sage wisdom
jokes.explanation: The setup feints at empathy ('it's actually really sad') before pivoting hard to Frank's signature brutal nihilism. The phrase 'piece of shit' applied to a human brain is jarring and funny in Frank's voice. The faux-sorrow setup makes the punchline land harder. High economy, high quotability, distinctly Frank. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What'd you do, did you, like, yank it out in a fit of rage? That's pretty psycho...

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: No... no, it's just genetics.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Aw, genetics, so psycho...!

jokes.text: Hey, I'm talking to my friends here, so... [Pete reveals himself as the person Charlie just told to get lost]
jokes.setup: Charlie is dismissing what he thinks is a random stranger interrupting, tells him to go get a beer
jokes.punchline: The stranger is Psycho Pete himself, whom they've been discussing — Charlie's rudeness to a random stranger is revealed as rudeness to the guest of honor
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom dramatic irony — the audience and others know something Charlie doesn't. Works efficiently and sets up the visual comedy of Pete's transformation. The rewatch value comes from catching the moment Charlie tells a cannibal to 'go have a beer, freak.'

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: struggling with my weight for a while now, yeah; M-meds don't help.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, oh, yeah, uh... A psycho struggle!

jokes.text: "There is no way we're having that psychotic mutant anywhere near our bar" — then Pete is immediately standing right there
jokes.setup: Dennis finishes a rant about how Pete cannot be allowed near the bar
jokes.punchline: Pete is already standing there, having heard it all, and Dennis doesn't recognize him
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom timing gag — the person being talked about walks in. It's a familiar structure but executed cleanly. The added layer that Dennis doesn't recognize him at all elevates it slightly.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Actually, you know, j-just turn the music down, j-just a bit.

jokes.text: What happened to your hair? You used to have all that hair. What'd you do, did you, like, yank it out in a fit of rage? That's pretty psycho... No... no, it's just genetics. Aw, genetics, so psycho...!
jokes.setup: Pete has visibly changed physically — heavier, different hair — since his institutionalization
jokes.punchline: Mac keeps trying to reframe mundane explanations (genetics, medication) as evidence of psycho behavior
jokes.explanation: Mac's refusal to accept normal explanations — finding the 'psycho' in everything — is a good running bit. 'Aw, genetics, so psycho!' is the highlight. It's repetitive by design but doesn't overstay its welcome. Good character work for Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Remember, like, you used to go right up to babies in carriages and just scream in their faces, you know, they'd cry...?

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: I-I don't feel good about that stuff. I actually regret a lot of the stuff we used to do.

jokes.text: "No, it's just genetics." / "Aw, genetics, so psycho!"
jokes.setup: Pete explains his hair loss is genetic
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately reframes 'genetics' as psycho — total commitment to delusion
jokes.explanation: "Aw, genetics, so psycho!" is a sharp, economical line. The rhythm of Pete giving a totally normal answer and Mac immediately co-opting it is the comedic engine of the whole reunion scene, and this exchange is the best iteration of it. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: This guy sucks now.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, my God.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Like, I don't like him at all.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, no, he's, like, not psycho at all.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, it's like Mild Mannered Pete.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: More like Boring Pete.

jokes.text: What are they feeding you, bro? I mean, you look huge; Look at that mass, it's great!
jokes.setup: Pete has gained weight due to medication side effects
jokes.punchline: Mac, who is obsessed with his own physique, admires Pete's medication-induced weight gain as impressive muscle mass
jokes.explanation: Mac's gym-bro lens applied to medication weight gain is funny. Calling it 'mass' and 'great' while Pete struggles with his meds is dark and character-specific. Not a standout but solid.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Sorry about the stuff I was saying about, uh... the mentally insane... earlier. Did that anger you? ...I didn't mean to call... psychotic people 'mutants.'

jokes.text: ♪ Come on, ride the train ♪ [Mac and Dennis do the freight train dance as a greeting for Pete, who declines]
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have hyped up 'getting the freight train back together' as a glorious reunion
jokes.punchline: Pete, clearly changed and subdued, asks them to just turn the music down — the grand reunion falls completely flat
jokes.explanation: The deflation of Mac and Dennis's excitement by Pete's quiet 'can you just turn the music down' is well-structured. The gap between their anticipation and Pete's subdued reality is the core joke of the episode and this is its first full delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: the main problem with people going to these state-run loony bins is the separation between church and state... You spend most of your time talking to a therapist, instead of a priest.

jokes.text: Remember, like, you used to go right up to babies in carriages and just scream in their faces, you know, they'd cry? Dude, that was psycho... I-I don't feel good about that stuff. I actually regret a lot of the stuff we used to do.
jokes.setup: Mac tries to reminisce about Psycho Pete's greatest hits to reignite the old dynamic
jokes.punchline: Pete expresses genuine remorse; Mac is visibly disappointed that screaming at babies is now off the table
jokes.explanation: Mac's 'dude, that was psycho' as a compliment while Pete expresses therapy-induced remorse is sharp. The juxtaposition of Mac's nostalgia for infant-terrorizing with Pete's growth is a clean comedic beat. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: a priest is gonna let you off the hook for all the things that you've done... He needs to be absolved, so that he can go psycho again.

jokes.text: This guy sucks now. Oh, my God. Like, I don't like him at all. No, no, he's, like, not psycho at all. No, it's like Mild Mannered Pete. More like Boring Pete.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis step away to privately assess the new, rehabilitated Pete
jokes.punchline: Their critique is entirely about Pete being 'boring' — not dangerous — culminating in 'More like Boring Pete'
jokes.explanation: Their disappointment is entirely selfish — not relief that he's better, but frustration he's no longer fun. 'Mild Mannered Pete / Boring Pete' as rebranding is a nice comedic escalation. This beat crystallizes the gang's sociopathy without overexplaining it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Holy shit, holy shit!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, shit, what happened? Put it on, put it on.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Put it back on! Put it back on!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What the hell happened to your face?!

jokes.text: "That's a good plan." — Charlie's response to Mac's plan of simply leaving
jokes.setup: Mac's plan for dealing with Pete is literally just 'We're gonna go'
jokes.punchline: Charlie's earnest endorsement of this non-plan as a 'good plan'
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean beat. The gang's social incompetence rendered in two words.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: This happened to me when I was locked in your burning apartment at Thanksgiving.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, you weren't there for that...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't think you were there, man.

jokes.text: I got a plan. [pause] We're gonna go. [Pete] Okay. [Dennis] That's a good plan.
jokes.setup: Dennis announces he has a plan for the Psycho Pete problem
jokes.punchline: The plan is simply to leave Pete alone with his glass of water — delivered and accepted with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. Dennis builds up 'I got a plan' with gravitas, then the plan is just 'leave.' Pete's quiet 'okay' and Dennis's self-satisfied 'that's a good plan' are the whole joke. No wasted words.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Why would we want you at Thanksgiving dinner? Especially looking like that, you would've freaked everyone out

jokes.text: Sorry about the stuff I was saying about, uh... the mentally insane... Did that anger you? ...earlier. I didn't mean to call... psychotic people 'mutants.'
jokes.setup: Dee realizes she was vehemently ranting about not wanting 'psychotic mutants' near the bar — directly in front of Pete
jokes.punchline: Her apology is broken, halting, and self-undermining — she keeps digging the hole while trying to fill it
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe apology that makes things worse. The fragmented delivery ('Did that anger you?') implies she's reading Pete's affect for danger signals. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: I don't need to suck him or anything or... let him inside me?

jokes.text: Charlie, you know, the main problem with people going to these state-run loony bins is the separation between church and state. [Charlie] Explain. Well, you spend most of your time talking to a therapist, instead of a priest.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie discuss why Pete isn't acting like his old self
jokes.punchline: Mac's diagnosis is that the problem is church-state separation — a priest would have let Pete 'off the hook' so he could 'go psycho again'
jokes.explanation: Mac's Catholic logic applied to mental health rehabilitation is a sharp piece of character writing. The idea that absolution (not therapy) is the proper treatment for murdering your family, delivered with total conviction, is exactly Mac's brand of confident wrongness. High character integration — this joke couldn't work without Mac's specific religious zealotry.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: if he wants up inside me, it will cost you a whole sixer, I mean, that... I got my dignity.

jokes.text: Look, dude, I feel guilty all the time for my thoughts and urges, you know, but I'm not gonna talk to a therapist, who's gonna make me, you know, deal with it and confront those issues. I talk to a priest, he lets me off the hook, I move on.
jokes.setup: Mac is explaining his philosophy on mental health treatment
jokes.punchline: Mac admits he has dark 'thoughts and urges' but prefers confession over therapy specifically because confession requires no actual change
jokes.explanation: The accidental self-revelation — Mac describes why he personally prefers confession to therapy while ostensibly talking about Pete — is excellent. The key insight ('he lets me off the hook, I move on') is a perfect encapsulation of Mac's moral dodge system. The 'thoughts and urges' line is a dark undertone that savvy viewers will clock.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: so they just cut all the loonies loose?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What? How could they do that? That's-that's insane!

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I guess it was either that or raise our taxes.

jokes.text: What do you guys want, huh? Can we ever get a warm reception from you? Yeah, it's never a nice 'hello.' What's the cloak thing, too? What are you doing here, like, a Phantom of the Opera thing... or what's the story? I don't like it, take it off, we want to talk to you. Pop it off, we're trying to have a conversation.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie approach Cricket, who is wearing a cloak to hide his disfigured face
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie complain about Cricket's unfriendly reception and his suspicious cloak — apparently unaware of the obvious reason he's wearing it
jokes.explanation: The setup is good — their obliviousness to why a disfigured person might cover their face is on-brand. The Phantom of the Opera reference is a nice touch. Mostly setup for the face reveal beat.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What?! Raise my taxes? Come on. How much do these vultures need? I already pay a ton in taxes... I'm not paying more in taxes, Dee. I won't do it. Don't speak of it again!

jokes.text: Holy shit, holy shit! Oh, shit, what happened? Put it on, put it on! Put it back on!
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie insisted Cricket remove his cloak
jokes.punchline: Cricket's severely burned face is revealed and they immediately beg him to put the cloak back on
jokes.explanation: The reversal — demanding the cloak come off then immediately demanding it go back on — is a crisp visual comedy beat. Well-structured with good rewatch value as it sets up the ongoing Cricket subplot. The reaction is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's okay, Froggy. I'll keep you moist.

jokes.text: This happened to me when I was locked in your burning apartment at Thanksgiving. I don't think you were there, man. I was there, Mac, and my whole face burned off. Why would we want you at Thanksgiving dinner? Especially looking like that, you would've freaked everyone out...
jokes.setup: Cricket explains his disfigurement was caused by Mac and Charlie's actions
jokes.punchline: Mac's response to 'I burned my face off at your apartment' is not guilt — it's confusion about why Cricket would have been invited, then blaming Cricket's burned face for why he wasn't invited
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The escalating logic — (1) we didn't invite you, (2) wait, your burned face would have freaked people out — retroactively applies the disfigurement they CAUSED as the reason he wouldn't have been invited. The circular cruelty is exquisite and perfectly in character. Mac's obliviousness to the causality is the dark heart of the show.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Th-This is the nitwit school I was shanghaied to when I was a kid... That one that you had your mommy tell them to tell you that you didn't have donkey brains.

jokes.text: I can't follow a thing this guy's saying... [Cricket clearly explaining cause and effect that couldn't be simpler]
jokes.setup: Cricket is making a completely coherent point about Mac causing his disfigurement
jokes.punchline: Mac genuinely cannot follow the logic, implying his sociopathy prevents him from processing causal responsibility
jokes.explanation: Mac's inability to follow a simple causal chain is funnier in context than it sounds — it implies his brain simply doesn't have a module for 'I caused harm.' Good character beat, solid but not standout.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: One time, we escaped and they chased us down with those big nets they use to catch dogs.

jokes.text: Hey, we brought you beer. Beer? Yeah, okay, fine, I'll help you; Just give me the beers. [gang holds them back] There's five more there. What about the others? They're not all for you, greedy.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie brought beers as currency to get Cricket's help
jokes.punchline: Cricket's total desperation reduced to negotiating over individual beer cans, while the gang haggles about how many he deserves
jokes.explanation: Cricket's transactional desperation (beer as currency) is well-established in the show. The gang treating a few cans of beer as a lavish payment for a priestly service is funny. 'Greedy' from Mac is a nice hypocrisy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Did you grow up in a cartoon?

jokes.text: Okay, we need you to hear our friend's confession and then absolve him of his sins. And? That's the whole thing, that's what priests do, right? Yeah, that's it. That's it? I don't need to suck him or anything or... let him inside me?
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie explain they just need a simple confession/absolution
jokes.punchline: Cricket's default assumption is that any interaction will involve sexual service — he's surprised when it doesn't
jokes.explanation: Cricket's fallen state is so far below rock bottom that a standard priestly service surprises him. The specific phrasing ('let him inside me') is blunt in a way that makes it funnier. Good character integration — only Cricket would go there.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: they used that money to open up the Eagles' new practice facility...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's kind of a no-brainer... you can't have our guys out there twisting ankles...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: A man of Shady McCoy's abilities, he needs a proper landing strip.

jokes.text: All right, yeah, but if he wants up inside me, it will cost you a whole sixer, I mean, that... I got my dignity.
jokes.setup: Cricket has just offered the possibility of sexual services
jokes.punchline: Cricket reasserts dignity — but his dignity has a price point (a six-pack)
jokes.explanation: 'I got my dignity' as the punchline after offering to let someone 'up inside him' for a six-pack is a perfect Cricket line. The word 'dignity' landing on what is objectively a deeply undignified position is the essence of his character. Highly quotable, well-constructed, and distinctly Cricket.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Sophie's choice, huh?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Mm-hmm.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oof. Go, Birds.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Go, Birds.

jokes.text: Oh, so they just cut all the loonies loose? What? How could they do that? That's-that's insane! I guess it was either that or raise our taxes. What?! Raise my taxes? Come on. How much do these vultures need? I already pay a ton in taxes.
jokes.setup: The mental institution has been shut down due to budget cuts
jokes.punchline: Dennis is outraged that dangerous mentally ill people were released — until the alternative (higher taxes) is raised, at which point he immediately sides with the budget cuts
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's sharpest piece of satirical writing. Dennis flips his position instantly the moment personal cost is mentioned, with no self-awareness. The escalating back-and-forth — 'What?! / Well then we'll shut down more. / WHAT?!' — is structurally excellent and builds with perfect rhythm. It's pointed political comedy about NIMBY attitudes dressed as character work.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Is that a glory hole?

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Yes. It is, my son. But it'll cost you a whole sixer if you want to unburden yourself in that way.

jokes.text: Well, then, we're going to have to pay more in taxes. What?! I'm not paying more in taxes, Dee. I won't do it. Don't speak of it again!
jokes.setup: Dennis has just argued we can't close mental institutions, so we need somewhere to send the mentally ill
jokes.punchline: The only logical solution requires him to pay more taxes, which he refuses to countenance — concluding with the absurd royal decree 'Don't speak of it again'
jokes.explanation: 'Don't speak of it again' as a way to close an argument he can't win is a great Dennis line. It's the logical conclusion of his self-serving reasoning and delivered with the pomposity that defines the character. Escalates joke 24 nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: he used to, um, scream in baby's faces.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Well, that's just funny. That was just plain funny...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Okay, no, you know what he used to do? He used to gather, like, cats and dogs... and then put them into like a little room and, like, have 'em battle it out.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: That's just cats' and dogs' nature, to fight, so I don't see a problem with that.

jokes.text: ♪ Rockabye Froggy On the treetop... ♪ [Frank singing a lullaby to something]
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee arrive at what turns out to be the nitwit school Frank attended as a child
jokes.punchline: Frank is tenderly singing a lullaby, apparently to 'Froggy' — a companion whose nature is not yet clear
jokes.explanation: The image of Frank tenderly singing 'Rockabye Froggy' is a great absurdist beat that becomes much funnier in retrospect once we learn Froggy is Frank's imaginary identity. Good rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: All right, um... he used to, um, scream in baby's faces.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Well, that's just funny. That was just plain funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I know, I know, I know.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: They'd be all freaked out...

jokes.text: It's okay, Froggy. I'll keep you moist.
jokes.setup: Frank is tenderly caring for 'Froggy' at the nitwit school
jokes.punchline: 'I'll keep you moist' — delivered with the earnest tenderness of a parent, applied to a frog person
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedy. 'I'll keep you moist' as a promise of care is bizarre, tender, and deeply weird. It becomes the episode's most quotable line and a callback anchor. Perfect economy. The word 'moist' doing enormous heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: also, he murdered and ate his family.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Right.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Jesus Christ! That guy's a goddamn maniac! I'm not absolving him!

jokes.text: That one that you had your mommy tell them to tell you that you didn't have donkey brains. I knew I didn't have donkey brains. But everybody else did.
jokes.setup: Frank recognizes the institution as the 'nitwit school' he attended as a child
jokes.punchline: Dee casually references the story of Frank's mom having to reassure the institution Frank didn't have 'donkey brains' — Frank's dignified response is 'I knew I didn't have donkey brains. But everybody else did.'
jokes.explanation: 'Donkey brains' as a clinical-sounding diagnosis is funny on its own. Frank's dignified clarification — that everyone else there had donkey brains, just not him — is a perfect Frank beat. The specificity of 'donkey brains' elevates it above generic 'you were called dumb' jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: there's a storm brewing on the inside... He's straight-up possessed by the devil... He used to be fun crazy... then the devil was like, 'I like this dude! I'm gonna get involved!'

jokes.text: Did you grow up in a cartoon?
jokes.setup: Frank has just described an escape attempt where he and his friend were chased by staff with large nets 'like the ones they use to catch dogs'
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat 'Did you grow up in a cartoon?' perfectly encapsulates how absurd Frank's childhood sounds
jokes.explanation: Five words that work perfectly as a straight-man reaction to absurdist escalation. The timing is excellent — Dee as voice of reason asking if Frank grew up in a Looney Tunes cartoon lands as one of the episode's best lines. Maximum economy, strong structure, earned reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Get the demon, the goblin, the ghoul and then you got Pete.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, no, no, no, no. There's no goblins, there's no ghouls, it's just demons, okay?

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Well, they're all made up, so...

jokes.text: That makes sense. That's kind of a no-brainer. I mean, you can't have our guys out there twisting ankles. A man of Shady McCoy's abilities, he needs a proper landing strip. Gotta get our maniacs in green set up in a nice facility.
jokes.setup: Dennis just discovered tax money for mental health went to the Eagles
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately agrees this was the right call — 'that's kind of a no-brainer' — and advocates passionately for the Eagles facility over mental health care using football metaphors
jokes.explanation: Dennis's instant pivot from outrage to full endorsement is excellent. 'Our maniacs in green' as a parallel to the actual maniacs they're trying to institutionalize is unspoken but sharp. The Eagles obsession as a blind spot for otherwise-expressed civic concern is good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'll act crazy and then he'll prescribe them to me.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Your bad acting will only confuse him and it will infuriate me.

jokes.text: "Gotta get our maniacs in green set up in a nice facility." / "Sophie's choice, huh?" / "Go, Birds." / "Go, Birds." / "Go, Birds."
jokes.setup: They've just been talking about releasing mentally ill people onto the streets
jokes.punchline: All three spontaneously rally around the Eagles — 'Sophie's choice' between mental health care and football said with complete sincerity, then the triple 'Go, Birds'
jokes.explanation: "Sophie's choice" applied to football vs. mental health is very sharp, and the triple 'Go, Birds' landing is a great button. The Philadelphia specificity makes this land especially well for local audiences and is a good example of place-specific character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Do you have some sort of donkey brain database?
No.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm looking for a kid, the frog kid. Just search for any half-man, half-amphibious creature.

jokes.text: Sophie's choice, huh? Mm-hmm. Oof. Go, Birds. Go, Birds. Go, Birds.
jokes.setup: They've just agreed that Eagles practice facilities are worth more than mental health infrastructure
jokes.punchline: 'Sophie's choice' applied to 'Eagles facility or mental health care' — then punctuated with sincere 'Go, Birds' from both
jokes.explanation: Using 'Sophie's choice' — a reference to an agonizing life-or-death wartime decision — to describe choosing Eagles funding over mental health care, then immediately sycophantically chanting 'Go, Birds' is a sharp, economical satirical joke. The triple 'Go, Birds' landing is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I've always relied upon the kindness of strangers.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What is... what are you do... What is that, A Streetcar Named Desire?

jokes.text: [Cricket speaking in a deep, reverbed priest voice through a confessional setup] Is there something weighing on your mind, my son?
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have set up an improvised confessional for Pete with Cricket as priest
jokes.punchline: Cricket, a defrocked priest who lives on the streets and was just negotiating beer-for-sexual-services, is now performing solemn priestly theater
jokes.explanation: Cricket's transformation into solemn priest mode is funny given what we just saw him doing. The theatricality of 'Is there something weighing on your mind, my son?' from a burned, street-dwelling ex-priest is a good visual/character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You haven't thought of the smell, you bitch!

jokes.text: It's time to confess your sins. Unburden yourself and be absolved. [Pete] Is that a glory hole? [Cricket] Yes. It is, my son. But it'll cost you a whole sixer if you want to unburden yourself in that way.
jokes.setup: Cricket has set up a confessional booth but it has a hole in the wall — Pete reasonably wonders what the hole is
jokes.punchline: Cricket confirms it's a glory hole and offers its services — but with the dignity of a pricing menu
jokes.explanation: The confessional glory hole is a great bit — the collision of sacred (confession) and profane (glory hole) in one physical object, managed by a defrocked priest, is conceptually brilliant. 'Yes. It is, my son.' delivers the confirmation with priestly solemnity, which makes it funnier. The pricing callback adds layers.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Of course I'm not, Dee. Don't be ridiculous. Think of the smell. You haven't thought of the smell, you bitch!

jokes.text: Uh... that being said, I'm... open to it.
jokes.setup: Pete has been presented with a glory hole in what he thought was a confessional
jokes.punchline: Pete, presented as the sane/rehabilitated member of the group, quietly considers using the glory hole
jokes.explanation: The understated delivery undercuts Pete's status as the 'normal' one. Perfect economy — 'that being said' doing all the work. The pause implied by 'uh...' makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Zimmerman
dialogue.line: you are Froggy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Huh?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Zimmerman
dialogue.line: It was you, Frank! You are the frog kid!

jokes.text: All right, um... he used to, um, scream in baby's faces. Well, that's just funny. That was just plain funny. I know, I know, I know. They'd be all freaked out...
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are trying to confess Pete's sins on his behalf because Pete won't do it himself
jokes.punchline: Cricket, the defrocked priest, doesn't see screaming at babies as a sin — 'that's just funny'
jokes.explanation: Cricket's moral framework — that screaming at babies is 'just funny, plain funny' — aligns him unexpectedly with Mac's earlier sentiment. This callback deepens the joke about how morally skewed everyone in this world is.

dialogue.line: You were an outcast as a child, so you created an imaginary friend... But the lines of reality became blurred. Soon you didn't know where Frank began and Froggy ended.

jokes.text: Also, he murdered and ate his family. Right. What? See, there was like a Christmas dinner thing with, like, the eating of his family and a burning of the house down.
jokes.setup: Mac is listing Pete's sins in a confessional, escalating from mild to extreme
jokes.punchline: Mac mentions murder and cannibalism with the same casual energy as screaming at babies, then has to summarize it as 'a Christmas dinner thing'
jokes.explanation: 'A Christmas dinner thing with the eating of his family' is an excellent euphemism for cannibalism. The understatement of 'thing' applied to murdering your family is a sharp dark comedy beat. Mac's matter-of-fact tone sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We have to catch the froggy.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Zimmerman
dialogue.line: Put that down. Get out of here!

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Zimmerman
dialogue.line: Here we go, come on...

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Zimmerman
dialogue.line: I'm not sick anymore! I'm not a frog!

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Zimmerman
dialogue.line: I know I'm not a frog!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Catch the froggy!

jokes.text: Jesus Christ! That guy's a goddamn maniac! I'm not absolving him! He should be in jail!
jokes.setup: Cricket discovers the person he's supposed to absolve is Psycho Pete, a confirmed cannibal
jokes.punchline: Cricket — a defrocked street priest who was just offering glory hole services and has had his face burned off by these same people — suddenly has standards about who deserves absolution
jokes.explanation: Cricket having a moral line he won't cross — from the depths of his degradation — is both funny and an unexpected character moment. The irony of Cricket, specifically, refusing to help a 'goddamn maniac' while standing in a glory hole confessional is rich. The outrage is completely genuine, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Unless you have crack. If you have crack, let's boogie.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No one is going into your asshole.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: I wouldn't let them without the crack.

jokes.text: [Pete enters, sees the confessional setup and Cricket] Hey, guys? Pete, is that you? I'm gonna get out of here, okay? Oh... I'm gonna use... use the women's restroom. Oh, sure! Yeah, a lot of people in here. Kind of a full house.
jokes.setup: Pete walks in on the improvised confessional, Cricket's burned face, and the general chaos
jokes.punchline: Pete politely excuses himself to the women's restroom; Mac and Charlie casually cover as if this is normal bar activity ('a lot of people in here, kind of a full house')
jokes.explanation: Mac's breezy social cover ('kind of a full house') for a deeply weird situation is a solid cringe beat. Pete's quiet retreat to the women's bathroom is a good reaction, but the scene is mostly transitional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, I had a simple conversation with a reasonable man and that man wrote me a prescription.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Mm, yeah. He got the drugs by being a real-life actual psychopath.

jokes.text: No, look, he-he might look calm on the outside, but there's a storm brewing on the inside, okay? And I think I know what the problem is. He's psycho. He's straight-up possessed by the devil.
jokes.setup: Mac tells Cricket to relax, Pete is docile and on meds
jokes.punchline: Cricket's expert diagnosis: Pete is 'straight-up possessed by the devil'
jokes.explanation: Cricket's theological framework for mental illness ('the devil made him do it') mirrors Mac's church-state argument from earlier. The earnestness of the diagnosis is funny but not exceptional — it's setup for the exorcism plan.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: All that stuff with my family? It's just, it's just a rumor people started about me... none of it was true, and then the more people spread it around, the more afraid people were of me.

jokes.text: Mac's escalating demonology: "the devil... then the meds get thrown on top... we gotta get him off the meds and get the devil out."
jokes.setup: Mac is building a theory of Pete's spiritual/pharmacological situation
jokes.punchline: His theory merges pharmacology and demonology with complete confidence — the meds are suppressing the devil, so removing them will free the fun demon
jokes.explanation: Mac's theory is genuinely well-constructed absurdism — the idea that the meds are suppressing a good devil (who made Pete fun-crazy) is a coherent internal logic that only Mac could arrive at.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Social anxiety disorder mixed with depression. I was really more of a danger to myself. I was always talking about committing suicide.

jokes.text: He used to be fun crazy. And the devil was like, 'I like this dude! I'm gonna get involved!' He jumps in there, makes him evil crazy, then the meds get thrown on top. They shut everybody down.
jokes.setup: Cricket is explaining his theory of Pete's psychological deterioration
jokes.punchline: The devil operates like an enthusiastic friend who wants to 'get involved' with someone cool — informal, conversational, jumping on a fun trend
jokes.explanation: Cricket's characterization of the devil as a hype-man who gets excited about a cool person and 'jumps in there' is genuinely funny absurdist theology. The colloquial voice given to Satan ('I like this dude!') is a creative and character-specific comedic choice.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: you always liked me, so I figured you guys could help me cope with it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That we would help...?

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Yeah!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah, yeah. Oh, yeah.

jokes.text: You want to do an exorcism? Of course I want to do an exorcism. That's what the... I was hoping... why didn't you just come right out here and be like, 'Let's do an exorcism'? I-I can't lead with the exorcism.
jokes.setup: Cricket's solution is an exorcism; Mac and Cricket agree with unusual enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: 'I can't lead with the exorcism' — Cricket reveals he has a social etiquette for escalating to exorcism requests
jokes.explanation: 'I can't lead with the exorcism' is one of the episode's best lines. It implies a social protocol where the exorcism is the logical endpoint but must be built up to through intermediate steps, as if it's a reasonable but big ask. The mutual enthusiasm from both Mac and Cricket for the exorcism plan is also funny — two broken people excited to do something genuinely insane.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: This thing's going all the way to Los Angeles, buddy, all right? City of Angels!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, a place where no one is depressed.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, you can surf the sadness away!

jokes.text: Oh, we should get 'em all out. Get the demon, the goblin, the ghoul and then you got Pete. Well, no, no, no, no. There's no goblins, there's no ghouls, it's just demons, okay? Well, they're all made up, so...
jokes.setup: Cricket specifies demons need to be exorcised; Mac wants to expand the scope to goblins and ghouls
jokes.punchline: Cricket, the expert, corrects Mac — no goblins or ghouls, just demons. Mac's rebuttal: 'they're all made up, so...'
jokes.explanation: Mac's 'they're all made up, so...' is a rare moment of Mac accidentally stumbling into rationalism while arguing for the wrong side of an argument. The logic is perfect: Mac uses reason to argue that fantasy creatures are interchangeable because none are real — while still believing in the exorcism. It's absurdist and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Train Conductor
dialogue.line: Oh, well, George, good luck. Enjoy Philadelphia, City of Brotherly Love.
Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Train Conductor
dialogue.line: They're gonna take great care of you here.

jokes.text: That's why he burned your face, you son of a bitch! Yeah, yeah, that's true, man!
jokes.setup: Cricket questioned whether demons and goblins are real
jokes.punchline: Mac blames Cricket's burned face on Cricket's skepticism about supernatural entities — and Cricket agrees
jokes.explanation: Mac's ability to fold any evidence into his worldview — including Cricket's fire-caused disfigurement — as proof of demonic activity is on-brand. Cricket's immediate agreement is sad and funny. The exchange is quick and efficient.

jokes.text: Let's just go get the exorcism going. All right, yeah, and let's get you, like, a hat or a hood or...
jokes.setup: They're concluding plans for the exorcism
jokes.punchline: Mac's afterthought concern is not the insane plan they've just agreed on, but Cricket's visual appearance — tacking on 'get you a hat or a hood' as an afterthought
jokes.explanation: Minor button on the scene — Mac prioritizing Cricket's aesthetics over the insane plan. Functional humor, not standout.

jokes.text: "Just let me handle this, okay? I'll act crazy and then he'll prescribe them to me." / "Your bad acting will only confuse him and it will infuriate me."
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are trying to get Pete's psychiatric medication from a doctor
jokes.punchline: Dennis's plan is to fake mental illness; his dismissal of Dee's offer to help — 'your bad acting will only confuse him and infuriate me' — is classically Dennis
jokes.explanation: "Your bad acting will only confuse him and it will infuriate me" is a great Dennis line — condescending, specific, and self-aggrandizing. His confidence in his own psychological manipulation is well-characterized.

jokes.text: Just search for any half-man, half-amphibious creature.
jokes.setup: Frank is at the hospital asking for a 'frog kid' and the doctor has no idea what he's talking about
jokes.punchline: Frank's search parameters for a medical database are 'half-man, half-amphibious creature'
jokes.explanation: The clinical framing of 'half-man, half-amphibious creature' as a medical search parameter is funny precisely because Frank delivers it with total bureaucratic earnestness. Good economy and high character specificity.

jokes.text: Doctor... I've always relied upon the kindness of strangers.
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to manipulate the doctor into prescribing him medication
jokes.punchline: Dennis launches into a Blanche DuBois impression from A Streetcar Named Desire — a theatrical, absurd approach to getting prescription drugs
jokes.explanation: Dennis's choice of Blanche DuBois as a character to play when seeking sympathy is an interesting character reveal — he goes theatrical and high-status even in manipulative mode. The reference is specific enough to be funny without being completely obscure.

jokes.text: I'm in desperate need of medical intervention. You see, years ago I tried to burn my college roommate down to the box springs whilst she was sleeping. And now... I have a hankering to do it again.
jokes.setup: Dennis is performing a dramatic persona to manipulate a doctor
jokes.punchline: His fabricated mental illness confession is actually a plausible Dennis Reynolds story — 'tried to burn my college roommate down to the box springs' and 'now I have a hankering to do it again'
jokes.explanation: Dennis's 'fake' psychosis script is essentially an accurate description of Dennis Reynolds. 'Down to the box springs' is a specific, horrible detail that sounds horrifyingly real. 'I have a hankering to do it again' is the perfect dark twist. The ambiguity of whether this is a performance or a confession is exactly the Dennis character. One of the episode's best and most deeply character-integrated jokes. The word 'hankering' adds a Southern Gothic flavor that elevates it.

jokes.text: I swear you would be of more use to me if I skinned you and turned your skin into a lampshade. Or fashioned you into a piece of high-end luggage. I can even add you to my collection!
jokes.setup: Dennis is continuing his dramatic performance to seem unstable in front of the doctor
jokes.punchline: Dennis describes wanting to skin Dee and turn her into luxury goods — 'high-end luggage,' 'my collection' — with a connoisseur's sensibility
jokes.explanation: Dennis's serial killer threats are terrifying because they sound genuine. 'High-end luggage' and 'my collection' suggest Dennis already has a collection of skin goods, delivered as an aspirational consumer. The specificity is what makes it land — this isn't generic threatening, it's Dennis's particular brand of genteel monstrousness.

jokes.text: "I swear you would be of more use to me if I skinned you and turned your skin into a lampshade... fashioned you into a piece of high-end luggage... I can even add you to my collection!"
jokes.setup: Dennis is 'performing' mental illness for the doctor while Frank destroys his scheme
jokes.punchline: His threats to Dee escalate from lampshade to luggage to 'my collection' — each step more specific and disturbing, with the casual delivery of a shopper describing home decor
jokes.explanation: This is Dennis at his peak — the serial killer undertone of the show made explicit with perfect escalation. 'I can even add you to my collection' implies an ongoing skin-luggage collection, and 'Think of the smell, you bitch!' when Dee questions him is both a logical rejoinder and completely unhinged. The escalation from lampshade → luggage → collection is beautifully structured. Among the best Dennis moments in the episode. Very high character integration — this is ONLY Dennis.

jokes.text: Are you saying that you have a collection of skin luggage? Of course I'm not, Dee. Don't be ridiculous. Think of the smell. You haven't thought of the smell, you bitch!
jokes.setup: Dee reasonably asks if Dennis actually has a skin luggage collection
jokes.punchline: Dennis denies it — not on moral grounds, but because of the practical smell problem. Then attacks Dee for not having thought through the logistics
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. Dennis denies having a skin collection not because it's wrong, but because of the SMELL — implying he has thought extensively about skin collections and ruled them out for practical reasons. Then he attacks Dee for being naïve enough not to have considered the smell. 'You haven't thought of the smell, you bitch!' is an extraordinary line. It reveals Dennis has done detailed planning around human skin goods, positions him as the smart one for ruling it out, and weaponizes Dee's reasonable horror. Perfect character integration, brilliant structure, among the most quotable lines in the episode. This is what a 9+ score looks like.

jokes.text: Now that that's settled, we can have a normal conversation.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just delivered escalating threats to skin Dee and turn her into luggage
jokes.punchline: He transitions to 'normal conversation' as if the preceding unhinged monologue was just clearing the air
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Dennis monologue. The transition from 'I will dice you into a million pieces in a glass box on my mantel' to 'now we can have a normal conversation' is a clean deadpan beat. Very high economy.

jokes.text: [Frank speaks to Dr. Zimmerman] Of course I recognize you. [pause] Good, 'cause I got questions. What did you do with him? Where is he? Where is who? The frog kid. Froggy!
jokes.setup: Frank finds Dr. Zimmerman, the old administrator, to get information about Froggy
jokes.punchline: Frank demands information about 'the frog kid' with the intensity of a detective — and the doctor has no idea what he's talking about
jokes.explanation: Setup scene for the Froggy reveal. Frank's intensity about finding 'the frog kid' is funny but mostly functional — the payoff comes in the next beat.

jokes.text: But, Franklin... ...you are Froggy.
jokes.setup: Frank has been desperately trying to find his childhood companion 'Froggy' at the institution
jokes.punchline: The reveal: Frank IS Froggy. Frank created an imaginary identity as a child and lost track of which one was real
jokes.explanation: The 'you are Froggy' reveal lands with genuine comic force. It recontextualizes Frank's earlier singing and 'I'll keep you moist' as Frank talking to himself in a dissociated state. The delivery — 'But, Franklin...' — mirrors the classic therapy/soap opera reveal format. Well-structured payoff for the episode's secondary plot. High rewatch value as the earlier Froggy moments take on new meaning.

jokes.text: It's okay, Froggy. I'll keep you moist. [flashback recontextualization — Frank was talking to himself]
jokes.setup: Dr. Zimmerman has just revealed Frank IS Froggy
jokes.punchline: Callback to Frank's earlier 'I'll keep you moist' — now understood as Frank reassuring his own dissociated frog identity
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'I'll keep you moist' in the revelation context elevates both jokes retroactively. Frank promising to keep himself (his frog self) moist while in a dissociative episode is genuinely dark comedy at its best. This is the kind of structural payoff that elevates an episode above average.

jokes.text: "Soon you didn't know where Frank began and Froggy ended." — delivered completely sincerely by the doctor
jokes.setup: Doctor is explaining Frank's condition
jokes.punchline: The philosophical/psychological line about identity dissolution applied to the question of which person is the frog is delivered with complete clinical seriousness
jokes.explanation: The clinical framing of a Frank/frog identity crisis is well-delivered. The sincerity of the doctor's explanation applied to this absurd subject works.

jokes.text: "Oh, yeah. I see that. I remember that now." — Frank accepting that he is Froggy
jokes.setup: Doctor reveals Frank is Froggy
jokes.punchline: Frank's instant, calm acceptance — not denial or shock, but 'yeah, that makes sense' — is perfectly in character
jokes.explanation: Frank's equanimity about being an imaginary frog is excellent character work. His calm 'I remember that now' implies this is just another Tuesday for Frank. Very good economy.

jokes.text: What are you doing? You're having an episode again, Frank, aren't you? We got to catch the little froggy. Put that down. Get out of here! I'm not sick anymore! I'm not a frog! I know I'm not a frog! Catch the froggy!
jokes.setup: Frank has had the revelation but then immediately has another episode, reverting to 'catching the froggy'
jokes.punchline: Frank simultaneously insists 'I'm not a frog!' while his body physically chases a frog — unable to integrate the revelation
jokes.explanation: Frank's immediate relapse into a Froggy episode seconds after the reveal is a good escalation beat. The simultaneous denial and physical pursuit ('I'm not a frog!' while chasing one) is the joke — he knows cognitively but can't stop behaviorally.

jokes.text: Frank immediately begins having a frog episode in the doctor's office — trying to catch a 'froggy' and licking things
jokes.setup: Doctor warns Frank could have another episode
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately has an episode — the warning and the event are simultaneous, suggesting Frank is constantly on the edge
jokes.explanation: Frank going frog immediately after the reveal is a good physical comedy moment. The speed of the relapse — mid-conversation with the doctor — is well-executed.

jokes.text: Let's go through the, through the, through the, the checklist. Um, crucifix. I got it. Yeah. Got that. Holy water -- we got that. Yeah, we got all the stuff. We got the straps. We got everything, man.
jokes.setup: Mac and Cricket are preparing for Pete's exorcism
jokes.punchline: They have a full professional exorcism kit — crucifix, holy water, straps — prepared with the efficiency of a checklist
jokes.explanation: The pragmatic efficiency of exorcism preparation treated like a shopping list is funny. 'We got the straps' as matter-of-fact detail is a small highlight. Functional setup comedy.

jokes.text: So, what's the plan? We're just gonna, like, bum-rush this guy from behind or what? Whoa, whoa, guys, come on. No one is taking me from behind, all right? Unless you have crack. If you have crack, let's boogie.
jokes.setup: Mac is discussing the logistics of subduing Pete for the exorcism
jokes.punchline: Cricket's objection to being 'taken from behind' is immediately qualified: he would allow it for crack, and the qualifier comes with enthusiasm ('let's boogie')
jokes.explanation: Cricket's negotiated dignity — no to being taken from behind, yes if crack is involved — is a solid Cricket joke. 'Let's boogie' as the enthusiastic pivot is a funny word choice. Good character integration.

jokes.text: No one is going into your asshole. I wouldn't let them without the crack.
jokes.setup: Mac clarifies they're not planning sexual assault during the exorcism
jokes.punchline: Cricket reasserts his crack-based consent framework: without crack, no one enters his asshole; with crack, it's on the table
jokes.explanation: Extension of the previous joke. The callback deepens Cricket's rules but adds less than the original beat. Functional.

jokes.text: Let's just go through the basic beats, all right? Uh, talk a bunch of Latin. Yeah, that's me. I'll fake it. Wait, what do you mean you'll fake it? You don't, you don't know your Latin anymore...? No, no. Don't worry about it. I can sell anything, you know?
jokes.setup: Mac and Cricket are planning the exorcism procedure
jokes.punchline: Cricket, a former priest, doesn't know his Latin for the exorcism — he'll 'fake it.' His justification is street survival experience: 'You know how many times I fake on the streets?'
jokes.explanation: Cricket's street-survival skills being applied to religious ceremony is a great character beat. 'You know how many times I fake on the streets?' applied to Latin exorcism chanting is funny and deeply sad simultaneously. The logic — if you can fake things on the street you can fake an exorcism — is exactly Cricket's brand of lowered-expectations wisdom.

jokes.text: Cricket, just like anything we can do to have you not talk about, like, sucking penises or getting raped in the butt... It just keeps popping up.
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to run a professional exorcism
jokes.punchline: Cricket's sexual-degradation references keep derailing the planning; Mac acknowledges it; Cricket's response is 'It just keeps popping up' — which is itself a double entendre
jokes.explanation: 'It just keeps popping up' as Cricket's oblivious self-description of his sexual trauma references is a good bit. The inadvertent double entendre is well-deployed. Cricket's lack of self-awareness is the joke.

jokes.text: Oh! Oh! Hey, I got it. Problem solved. I got Pete's drugs. Oh, we got drugs? All right, crank me up, baby! We going up? Down? How we doing this, huh?
jokes.setup: Dennis arrives with Pete's prescription medication as a solution
jokes.punchline: Cricket instantly assumes the drugs are for recreational use and demands to know if they're uppers or downers
jokes.explanation: Cricket's drug-addict instinct kicking in immediately upon hearing 'drugs' is predictable but executed with enough energy to land. 'Crank me up, baby!' has a good texture.

jokes.text: "He had some sort of, like, Thanksgiving incident. God's wrath. He went to some, like, party... Yeah, at your house! Everyone was there! How do you not remember this?" / "I don't have a house!"
jokes.setup: Cricket tries to establish that his face was burned in their apartment
jokes.punchline: The gang continues to collectively misremember and deflect — 'I don't have a house!' is Frank's perfect non-answer
jokes.explanation: "I don't have a house!" is a great Frank non-sequitur defense — technically true, completely evasive. The escalating denial among all gang members is good collective character comedy.

jokes.text: What the hell is Crick...? Cricket! Jesus Christ! Oh, the face? Yeah, sorry. That is gross, man! What the hell?! He had some sort of, like, Thanksgiving incident. God's wrath. He went to some, like, party... Yeah, at your house! Everyone was there! How do you not remember this?
jokes.setup: Dennis sees Cricket's burned face for the first time in this episode
jokes.punchline: Mac describes it as 'some sort of Thanksgiving incident' — a gross understatement — and Cricket keeps insisting it happened at Mac's apartment, which Mac keeps denying
jokes.explanation: Return to the Cricket face gag with Dennis's fresh reaction and Mac's continued denial. 'God's wrath' as Mac's explanation is a small highlight (classic Mac religious deflection). Less impactful as a callback than the original revelation.

jokes.text: Well, I had a simple conversation with a reasonable man and that man wrote me a prescription. Mm, yeah. He got the drugs by being a real-life actual psychopath. No, the man asked me a few questions. I answered those questions as honestly as I could. Next thing I know I'm walking out the door with meds for borderline personality disorder.
jokes.setup: Dennis explains how he got Pete's medication
jokes.punchline: Dennis describes his psychopathic performance as 'answering questions honestly' — implying his real answers to standard psychiatric screening questions earned him a BPD diagnosis
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Dennis's 'performance' was just him being honest is one of the episode's best structural payoffs. Dee's framing — 'that's how you get diagnosed' — lands perfectly. This is the culmination of the Dennis doctor scene and it retroactively recontextualizes his entire 'act.' Dennis Reynolds as an undiagnosed BPD case is a long-running show thread and this joke honors that beautifully.

jokes.text: No, no. That's how you get diagnosed.
jokes.setup: Dennis claims his psych appointment method was just getting things done efficiently
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat correction: 'That's how you get diagnosed' — not congratulating his efficiency but noting he's been classified as mentally ill
jokes.explanation: Six words of perfect deadpan that land as the best button on the Dennis arc. The simplicity is what makes it devastating. Dee, often the butt of jokes, gets a genuinely excellent zinger here. Among the most economical punchlines in the episode.

jokes.text: "You see? That's how you get shit done, Dee." — Dennis, satisfied with himself after being diagnosed with borderline personality disorder
jokes.setup: Dennis has just unknowingly revealed he was genuinely diagnosed with BPD
jokes.punchline: He delivers this as a master class in getting things done — his self-satisfaction is completely disconnected from reality
jokes.explanation: Dennis's triumphant 'that's how you get shit done' as a button to being diagnosed with a personality disorder is excellent. His complete inability to understand what just happened is very high character integration — this is ONLY Dennis.

jokes.text: Whoa! Whoa! Whoa! I'm gonna put him out of his misery! No, no! Frank, Frank! We're gonna help this guy, all right? But there's no helping him, Dennis -- don't you understand?
jokes.setup: Frank arrives waving something, clearly having lost his grip on reality after the Froggy revelation
jokes.punchline: Frank's solution to Pete's mental illness is to 'put him out of his misery' — treating Pete like a sick animal
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'put him out of his misery' is a dark beat that works through Frank's post-Froggy fragility. His desperation is real which makes it funny-sad. Decent escalation setup for the Pete reveal.

jokes.text: I know. I'm the frog kid, right? It was all in my mind, but I got cured. But I could have another episode. So if I had another episode, what do I do? I eat a couple of flies. If he has another episode, he kills us. He's a murderer!
jokes.setup: Frank draws parallels between himself (cured Froggy) and Pete (dangerous when relapsing)
jokes.punchline: Frank's coping mechanism for a Froggy episode is eating a couple of flies — which he presents as equivalent to Pete's murder relapse
jokes.explanation: 'I eat a couple of flies' as Frank's relapse management plan is excellent. The logic — his episode = flies, Pete's episode = murder — is structurally perfect. The casual normality of fly-eating as a treatment plan is a great absurdist detail. Frank has fully integrated 'frog kid' into his identity.

jokes.text: No, no, really. All that stuff with my family? It's just, it's just a rumor people started about me. You know, kind of like all the rumors you guys started about me? What rumors? What are you talking about? You know, that I'm crazy and stuff.
jokes.setup: Frank and Dennis are preparing to handle 'dangerous murderer' Pete
jokes.punchline: Pete reveals the murder/cannibalism story was entirely a rumor — and implicitly, the gang spread and amplified it
jokes.explanation: The recontextualization of the entire episode's premise is the best structural joke in the episode. The gang has been treating a person with social anxiety and depression as a dangerous cannibal — and they helped create that reputation. The parallel to 'all the rumors you guys started about me' implicates them directly. It's the show's core thesis (the gang causes harm through thoughtlessness) delivered through a perfect structural reveal. The understated delivery makes it land harder than any explicit accusation would.

jokes.text: That's why I wanted to reconnect with you guys 'cause, you know, a lot of people they can't deal with that kind of stuff, but you always liked me, so I figured you guys could help me cope with it.
jokes.setup: Pete reveals he has social anxiety and depression and reached out to the gang for support
jokes.punchline: Pete's reason for trusting the gang — 'you always liked me' — is ironic given the gang spent the episode trying to exorcise him, drug him, and 'put him out of his misery'
jokes.explanation: Pete's trust in the gang as people who 'always liked him' is a devastating ironic beat. The audience knows everything the gang did this episode in his name. The cringe comes from the gap between Pete's sincere gratitude and the gang's actual behavior. Dark and well-structured.

jokes.text: That we would help...? Yeah! Oh, yeah, yeah. Oh, yeah. Well, we could help you cope with it. Um... Or... ♪ Come on, ride the train ♪
jokes.setup: Pete has just sincerely asked the gang for help with his depression and social anxiety
jokes.punchline: The gang briefly feigns consideration ('Oh, yeah, yeah') before immediately pivoting to the freight train song to send Pete away
jokes.explanation: The freight train song being repurposed from a welcome to a dismissal is a sharp callback. The 'Um... Or...' pause before the music hits is perfectly timed — a half-second of the gang considering actual compassion before defaulting to deflection. The 'Or' doing enormous narrative work.

jokes.text: This thing's going all the way to Los Angeles, buddy, all right? City of Angels! Yeah, a place where no one is depressed. Yeah, you can surf the sadness away!
jokes.setup: The gang is bundling Pete onto a freight train to get rid of him
jokes.punchline: Their solution to Pete's depression — Los Angeles, 'a place where no one is depressed,' 'surf the sadness away' — is both wildly wrong and perfectly self-serving
jokes.explanation: 'A place where no one is depressed' applied to Los Angeles is a good ironic joke (LA being famously rife with depression and mental illness in the entertainment industry). 'Surf the sadness away' is the kind of glib non-advice the gang would give someone in genuine crisis.

jokes.text: I just want to thank you guys so much for trying to help me. I suppose it could be good to get a fresh start.
jokes.setup: The gang has manipulated Pete into hopping a freight train to Los Angeles
jokes.punchline: Pete genuinely thanks them for 'trying to help' — unaware that everything they did was to get rid of him, not help him
jokes.explanation: Pete's sincere gratitude for being abandoned onto a freight train is the cringe culmination of the episode's main theme. The gang has successfully avoided helping someone who genuinely needed help while making him feel helped. Dark and well-executed.

jokes.text: Hey, listen. Save the chit-chat for the hobos. You got a long trip.
jokes.setup: Pete is thanking the gang warmly
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses Pete's heartfelt moment with 'save the chit-chat for the hobos' — sending him off to share a freight car with hobos
jokes.explanation: 'Save the chit-chat for the hobos' is a highly quotable, economical dismissal that also reveals Pete is literally being sent to ride with hobos. The casualness of Dennis solving a mental health crisis by putting a depressed person on a freight train with hobos to Los Angeles is a perfect Always Sunny button.

jokes.text: "All right, well, uh, you guys want to go pop by the new Eagles facility?" — immediately after solving the Pete problem
jokes.setup: They've just disposed of Pete
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately pivots to Eagles plans — tying back to the tax/Eagles thread and showing zero processing time between abandoning a friend and leisure activities
jokes.explanation: Good callback that ties the Eagles subplot to the resolution — the facility that was built instead of mental health care is now their fun destination. The thematic circularity is satisfying.

jokes.text: Oh, well, George, good luck. Enjoy Philadelphia, City of Brotherly Love. Yeah. They're gonna take great care of you here. Yeah, rain, rain, buzzing... All right, get on out of here. Take care, pal. Okay. Bye. Well, that takes care of that. Problem solved. Let's get out of here.
jokes.setup: In what appears to be a parallel or mirrored scene at a train station, Dennis and Frank are sending someone else away
jokes.punchline: They're sending someone to Philadelphia (where the show takes place) with the same dismissive efficiency — 'problem solved' — mirroring how Pete was handled, implying they do this constantly
jokes.explanation: The final scene reveals this is a pattern — the gang sends people away to 'solve problems' and receives people sent away by others in the same system. 'Enjoy Philadelphia, City of Brotherly Love' as an ironic welcome to the city the show depicts as a hellhole is a good meta joke. The 'problem solved' echo is a strong structural button.

jokes.text: "Oh, well, George, good luck. Enjoy Philadelphia, City of Brotherly Love." — Dennis sending off someone named George as the gang watches
jokes.setup: We think Dennis is wrapping up with Pete
jokes.punchline: Dennis is actually sending off someone else — 'George' — implying they've also put a second random person on the freight train
jokes.explanation: The final gag — there's a second person named George who is apparently being sent away from (or into) Philadelphia — is a good misdirection button. 'City of Brotherly Love' applied to what appears to be the gang disposing of another unwanted person is sharp irony. The episode ends on this unexplained George, which is very Always Sunny.

tmdb_overview: When Psycho Pete, long lost member of the freight train, is released from the mental hospital, Dennis and Dee rush to get him recommitted while Charlie and Mac attempt to restore him to his former hard-partying form.
